questions.q: Why do trading and pricing systems still reach for C++ instead of a garbage-collected language?
options: C++ is easier to learn than Python or Java
C++ gives direct, predictable control over memory and execution, avoiding GC pauses in the hot path
C++ has a larger standard numerical library than Python
Garbage collection is not possible on trading hardware
questions.explain: C++'s appeal in finance is predictable low-latency control over memory and execution, not ease of learning or library size — a garbage collector can pause a program at a time it chooses, which C++ avoids entirely.

questions.q: What does calling trades.reserve(1'000'000) before a loop of push_back calls accomplish?
options: It sorts the vector in advance
It pre-allocates capacity so push_back doesn't trigger unpredictable reallocations later
It fills the vector with one million default-constructed Trade objects
It makes the vector read-only
questions.explain: reserve() allocates capacity up front without adding elements, so subsequent push_back calls don't need to reallocate and copy — important for avoiding latency spikes.

questions.q: In the loop `for (const Trade& t : trades) { ... }`, why use `const Trade&` instead of `Trade`?
options: const Trade& is required syntax for all range-based for loops
It avoids copying each Trade just to read its fields
It makes the loop run in parallel automatically
Trade cannot be copied at all
questions.explain: Binding by const reference lets the loop read each element in place instead of making a copy of every Trade, which matters when the vector is large or iterated often.

questions.q: What does 'zero-overhead abstraction' mean in C++'s design philosophy?
options: Abstractions like classes and templates should cost nothing extra at runtime versus equivalent hand-written low-level code
The compiler is free to download at no cost
All C++ programs run in zero time
Abstractions are forbidden in performance-critical code
questions.explain: Zero-overhead abstraction means high-level, expressive code should compile down to the same performance as a hand-written lower-level equivalent — no hidden runtime tax for using classes, templates, or the STL.

questions.q: What determines when a local C++ object's destructor runs, in the absence of dynamic allocation?
options: A background garbage collector thread, on an unpredictable schedule
The object is destroyed when it goes out of scope
The operating system decides at process exit only
Destructors never run automatically in C++
questions.explain: C++ has no garbage collector; a local object's lifetime is tied to its scope, and its destructor runs deterministically when that scope ends.
